gap: None of ChatGPT's results gives a measured figure for the candidate kits: OutdoorGearLab got 910 Wh out of the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2, 950 Wh out of the BLUETTI AC180, 870 Wh out of the EcoFlow DELTA 3 and 230 Wh out of the Anker SOLIX C300, and its 200–220 W folding panels gave 150–193 W in clear sun, so one panel needs about 4.5–6.3 hours of ideal sun to refill a 1 kWh unit.
standout_why: I compared against PowerStationGearLab (cited), Flowers of Vice (cited), Wattfolk (#2) and The Gadgeteer (#6). PowerStationGearLab says 'we don't test products ourselves' and gives only listed capacities: no usable Wh, solar input, idle draw or dB. Flowers of Vice gives only ratings plus the author's own estimate of '850Wh usable'. Wattfolk says 'We did not hands-on test any product' and works yields from assumed factors. The Gadgeteer reports no measurements, only maker specs and estimates. ChatGPT's own answers use rated Wh and 'illustrative' daily yields. UrbanGridBackup (cited #1) would not open (certificate error), so I could not check it.
decides: The finding backs the 1 kWh class for outage backup, since all three tested 1 kWh units deliver about 85% of their rating (870–950 Wh). It also limits that advice: OutdoorGearLab's best panel managed 193 W, so a 1 kWh battery will not refill from one balcony panel in a typical day. For our compact pick, BLUETTI Elite 30 V2, The Technology Man measured 231 Wh usable on AC and about 19 W of idle inverter drain with Eco mode off. The page should tell renters to run an overnight router from DC or Eco mode, not from AC left on. The measurements do not change the order between the 1 kWh units: the AC180 delivered the most energy but was tested with the weakest panel.

findings.note: Cross-check: 19 W × 12 h = 228 Wh, and 81% of 288 Wh = 233 Wh, so the two figures agree. For a renter backing up a router overnight, AC idle alone would use roughly what one balcony panel adds in a good hour.
